# Tomato blight

## What happened this year

Plot 14 at the Wrey Valley allotments, polytunnel end. First sign on 3 August 2024: greasy olive patches on the lower leaves of the 'Ferline' plants nearest the door. By the 6th the stems had dark streaks about a thumb long and two trusses of green fruit had gone a mottled bronze, firm and dimpled, as if someone had pressed them with a dirty thumb. Classic late blight, Phytophthora infestans, the same beast that does the potatoes (see [[Potato late blight]]), but in the tunnel it turned up nearly a fortnight after the outdoor spuds went down.

I was cross with myself for a whole afternoon, then made a pot of tea and wrote this.

## The plants, for the record

- 'Ferline' x6 (F1, sold as blight tolerant, ha) - first to go
- 'Crimson Crush' x4 - held out until 14 August, then caught it on two plants only
- 'Sungold' x5 - never showed a single lesion. Cherry types seem to shrug it off, or perhaps they were just at the far end by the vents
- 'Gardener's Delight' x3 outdoors against the shed - finished by 9 August

Seed from Moles Seeds, order MS-40177, £14.85 for the lot including postage. Sown 2 March under the lights in the spare room.

## Weather before it struck

I keep max/min readings from the little white louvred box by the water trough. A Hutton Period is two days in a row with a minimum of at least 10°C and at least six hours of humidity at 90% or above. BlightWatch emailed a Hutton alert for TQ13 on 29 July. Rain on 31 July (14 mm) and 1 August (9 mm). The tunnel doors stayed shut on the 1st because Colin Prowse was away in Exmouth and I had the dentist in Newton Abbot at 11.20. That is the mistake, plain and simple: warm, shut, wet leaves.

## What I did

### Stripping leaves

Took everything off up to the first truss, then every leaf showing a spot. Secateurs dipped in Jeyes Fluid between plants (one capful to a 2 litre jug). Washed my hands at the trough after each row, which Colin thinks is overdoing it.

### Saving the fruit

Picked all green fruit bigger than a 10p piece. Dunked them in water at 50°C for 10 minutes (kitchen thermometer, kettle top-ups), dried on tea towels, then laid them out in egg boxes on the back windowsill. Of 4.2 kg picked, about 2.9 kg ripened clean. The remainder went soft and dark within the week and went out.

### Getting rid of it

Bagged and into the council green bin, not my own heap. The spores don't last long on dead leaves, but I'm not taking chances. The [[Compost pile]] runs hot enough some summers and not others.

## Why the tunnel didn't save them

I always thought the cover keeps the rain off the leaves and that's half the battle. It isn't, if the leaves sit wet with condensation from dawn until ten. Changes for next year:

1. Both ends open by 7 am from July, propped with the old brick.
2. Water at the roots only, on the drip line (notes in [[Drip irrigation]]).
3. Space plants 60 cm apart, not 45 cm. Fewer plants, more air.
4. Take the lower leaves off early, by mid July, whether or not anything shows.

## Varieties to try in 2025

'Crimson Crush' again, it earned its place. Adding 'Lizzano' and 'Primabella', both bred for blight resistance. Derek Yeo says 'Primabella' sold out at the Dartington plant sale by March, so order in January. Dropping 'Ferline' entirely.

## Kitchen end

Six jars of green tomato chutney from the stragglers that never coloured, labelled GTC-24 on the lids. Colin took a bag of the 'Sungold' for his [[Hot sauce mash]] experiment, which he says is "mostly tomato, a bit of chilli". It was mostly chilli.
